description: Returning after a layoff is a protocol, not a mood. Take today's honest push-up max, compare it with your best ever, and run the three-week ramp that respects the two calendars: muscle memory fast, tendons slow.

scenes.narration: Today's test has two parts, and the second part is a memory. Part one: push-ups, strict form, chest to the floor, full lockout, as many clean reps as you own today, stopping when the form breaks rather than when the ego does. That is your current number, and it must be honest or the whole episode is fiction. Part two: recall your best-ever max, from a log if you kept one, from memory if you did not, and write it beside today's figure. The gap between the two is the assignment. If you never actually left training, run the test anyway and treat the gap as zero; the protocol still has something for you at the end. This episode exists because comebacks are where motivated men get hurt and discouraged in the same fortnight: they train their memory of themselves instead of their current tissue, and the tissue files a complaint. The ramp that fixes it respects a simple biological fact the memory episode established: two systems return at two speeds, and the programme must be built for the slower one. Keep both numbers where you can see them. They are the before picture of the fastest progress of your training life.

beats.text: AN EXCHANGE RATE, NOT A JUDGEMENT

scenes.label: THE RETURNING LIFTER'S STARTING DOSE
scenes.narration: Here is the ramp's first number, and it feels insulting until you understand it. Week one of a comeback runs at roughly half of your old volume and load: half the sets, reps in reserve, sessions that end feeling suspiciously manageable. The insult is the point of confusion. Your muscles, staffed by the parked myonuclei from the memory episode, genuinely could do more, and they will tell you so by day three. Your tendons, joints, and connective tissue kept no such hardware; they deconditioned on the layoff's calendar and must be reloaded on theirs, which is measured in weeks of progressive strain, not in enthusiasm. Fifty percent is the dose that lets the fast system idle while the slow system rebuilds, and it lasts exactly one week. Men who skip it do not save time; they spend it, usually in week two, on an ache that a ramp would have priced at nothing. The number is not a judgement of your toughness.
scenes.sub: week one at half: the muscle complains it is easy - the tendons thank you

lines: The ramp reopens each at its speed.
beats.title: FULL MANAGEMENT, RUSTY LINES

scenes.narration: Recall the machinery that makes the ramp work, because a protocol believed is a protocol finished. During your first build, satellite cells donated nuclei to your growing fibres, and the evidence says many of those nuclei stayed through the layoff, parked inside the shrunken fibres like foremen in an empty factory. That is why the rebuild outruns the first build: protein production can restart at full staffing immediately, with no recruitment drive. The nervous system kept its own records too, which is why the movements feel clumsy for two sessions and then suddenly familiar, the software reloading faster than the hardware refills. What did not keep records is the connective tissue: tendons and ligaments thinned their collagen turnover down to match the quiet months, and their rebuilding signal, as the collagen episodes taught, answers to weeks of dosed strain. So the comeback body is a factory with full management, rusty supply lines, and a loading dock under repair. The ramp is simply the schedule that reopens all three at their own speeds.

The rebuild curve, as coaches observe it and the detraining literature sketches it, has a shape worth memorising. Strength returns first and fastest, riding the nervous system's relearning, often visibly within the first week. Size follows across weeks three to eight, as the refilled districts restore the fibre's full cross-section. The bars below show the typical comparison: the weeks a first build needs to reach a given level against the weeks the rebuild needs to return to it. Two honest caveats ride with the picture. The longer and more complete the layoff, the more the rebuild resembles a build; memory is a head start, not a teleport. And the first week's soreness will lie to you in both directions, feeling catastrophic on day two and gone by day six, because it is reporting novelty, not damage, exactly as the soreness episode explained.

The ramp itself, week by week, because this is the deep dive and details are the rent. Week one, fifty percent: your old movements, half the sets, every set stopped two or three reps before failure, sessions short enough to feel like a rehearsal. The goal is blood flow, technique reload, and soreness that teaches for a day, not a week. Week two, seventy percent: add the missing sets back, allow one genuinely hard set per movement, and let the nervous system remember what full recruitment feels like while the tendons take their second, still-modest, strain dose. Week three, eighty-five percent: near-full training, loads honest, the only thing withheld is the maximal test itself. Week four: retest, same push-up rules as today, and let the number grade the whole ramp. Running underneath all four weeks, the comeback supplements that actually exist: protein at every meal, because the foremen build only what deliveries bring, and sleep defended like a training session, because the rebuild's chemistry runs the night shift. That is the entire deep dive.

Price the comeback at your size and the advantage is almost unfair. Your best-ever numbers are bodyweight numbers, reps and seconds, which means the ramp needs no equipment, no loading calculations, and no spotter; the dose is counted in sets, and the vehicle is the same floor you tested on. The absolute gap to close is also small: a push-up max twenty reps below its peak is a three-week story, where the heavy lifter's comeback involves reintroducing hundreds of kilos to joints that have forgotten them, over months, with real risk priced into every ambitious session. And your feedback loop is faster: the gap is visible in the count within the first fortnight, and visible progress is the fuel comebacks run on. Men abandon ramps they cannot see working. Yours reports weekly, in the plainest numbers there are. Add the final dividend: because the whole protocol is bodyweight, it survives travel, schedule chaos, and the exact life disruptions that caused the layoff in the first place. The comeback that cannot be interrupted is the one that finishes.
Week-one rules, demonstrated now: submaximal push-ups, three rounds, stopping two reps before failure every time. Rehearsal pace, perfect form. Begin the ramp.

beats.text: EASY IS THE FAST SYSTEM TALKING
TEST YOUR MAX ON DAY ONE

scenes.narration: The comeback protocol, compressed to its rules. Rule one: log the old numbers before you start, today's max and best ever both, because a ramp without a destination is just wandering with good intentions. Rule two: follow the percentages even when they feel easy, especially when they feel easy; the easy feeling is the fast system talking, and the slow system does not get a vote until it aches, which is too late. Rule three: one hard test per comeback, at the end of week four, not a weekly referendum on your worth. Rule four: feed and sleep like the rebuild is your job for one month, because biologically it is, and the foremen are waiting on deliveries. Rule five: if a joint complains in a way that grows across sessions rather than fading, the ramp pauses and the complaint gets assessed; comebacks are long games and a paused week costs nothing next to a forced season. Five rules, three weeks of patience, and then the retest. The men who finish comebacks are not the most motivated.

So, your comeback verdict, read off the gap. Within twenty percent of your best: a short ramp, two to three weeks, and you are back on your old ground almost before the layoff feels real. Twenty to forty percent back: the classic distance, the full four-week protocol with its retest, arriving faster every week as the curve steepens. Beyond forty percent: a rebuild with a head start, six honest weeks, graded by the same ramp stretched over more ground, and still faster than any beginner alive could travel it. In every band, the instruction is identical: record both numbers where you will see them daily, because the closing gap is the most motivating chart in training and it only motivates if it is visible. Put your two numbers in the comments, today and best ever, side by side. In thirty days we retest, and the first number should be chasing the second at a speed that would be impossible if the memory were a myth. It is not a myth. It is nuclei, patience, and a ramp. Welcome back.
Thirty days from now, same strict push-ups, same honest count. Bring me a gap that is closing. Subscribe, and keep your numbers safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing muscle memory Wrong: Train Your muscle nuclei Instead
